speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head B of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, under Article 35(7), he is the chief legal advisor to the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is provided that the Attorney-General is to "advise the Government upon such legal matters and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him… and to discharge the functions conferred on him".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this advisory role, the Government is his client and it is the Government who will decide what should be done.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Attorney-General may have to take certain courses of action even if they go against his own advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, he has a pivotal public role in criminal matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 35(8) provides that the Attorney-General is the Public Prosecutor and vested with power, exercisable at his discretion, to institute, conduct or discontinue any proceedings for any offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The AG has the responsibility to decide on criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state: who should be charged, who should be let off with a warning, who should have their charges reduced or compounded and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He is arguably more powerful than a High Court judge, as his exercise of discretion is done in private and is unappealable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Public Prosecutor (PP), the Attorney-General is expected to be fiercely independent and have no hesitation to bring charges against the most powerful officeholders if the circumstances warrant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The rule of law, which we hold so dear, depends on it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe this separation exists in other countries to enhance the independence of the Public Prosecutor's office.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my understanding, the dual role of the Attorney-General was drafted into the Constitution at a time when our legal manpower was more limited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Already within the Attorney-General's Chambers organisation, besides the Attorney-General himself, we have two Deputy Attorneys-General and a Solicitor-General.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that we can assign the role of Public Prosecutor to the Attorney-General and the role of the Government's legal advisor to one of the Deputy Attorneys-General or to the Solicitor-General.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Constitution originally envisaged the Attorney-General to hold office until 60 years of age, and was later amended to allow Attorneys-General to hold office for a specific period.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the recent past, some Attorneys-General had held office for short terms of two to three years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I suggest that the Government introduce a minimum term of appointment to enable the Attorney-General to enjoy some security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about decoupling the dual roles of the Attorney-General as Public Prosecutor and also chief legal advisor to the Government, and granting security of tenure to this office, to strengthen the system, and also made reference to systems in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I understand the thrust of Ms Sylvia Lim's speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government fully agrees that public confidence is important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And because of the way we have built up our institutions, public confidence in our institutions is high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our institutions work well and have worked well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Survey statistics referred to during the 2016 Committee of Supply debates showed that public confidence in the legal system is, indeed, high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The public's confidence in the Attorney-General's Chambers did not develop by chance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was the result of prudent legal safeguards, as well as the integrity of those in the system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the Constitution itself has robust safeguards to protect the Attorney-General's independent exercise of prosecutorial discretion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It provides that the Attorney-General has the discretion "to institute, conduct or discontinue any proceedings for any offence".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both the President and the Prime Minister must agree on the appointment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Presidential veto contributes to a more robust system compared to other major common law jurisdictions which I believe is a reference point that Ms Sylvia Lim has taken, such as England and Wales, Australia and New Zealand, where the officers in charge of prosecutions in those countries are appointed solely by the government Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, the Attorney-General does not hold a political office.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This further reinforces the independence of the Attorney-General, and is also unlike other jurisdictions, such as England and Wales, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, where the Attorney-General holds a political office and is, therefore, subject to political pressures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Separation of the role of the Attorney-General from that of the Public Prosecutor in those jurisdictions is, therefore, necessary to ensure the independent exercise of prosecutorial discretion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Constitutional safeguards in Singapore ensure that the Attorney-General is protected from such pressures and allows him to discharge both his roles as Public Prosecutor as well as the Government's legal advisor without fear or favour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim suggested that the Public Prosecutor should have security of tenure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Again, if Members look at and compare our system with that of mature common law jurisdictions, the officers in charge of prosecutions in England and Wales, Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong do not have security of tenure and typically serve predetermined renewable terms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What is more important is that it is very difficult to remove the Attorney-General in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The President, the Prime Minister and a tribunal of three Judges, which must include the Chief Justice, must all agree that the Attorney-General is unable to discharge his functions, or that there has been misbehaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In some of the other mentioned jurisdictions, the requirements for removal are considerably less stringent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I am sure Ms Sylvia Lim knows that that alone cannot itself maintain public trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Attorney-General Lucien Wong recently said that the Attorney-General's independence is "enshrined in the Constitution and is an established rule of practice within Chambers".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Attorney-General has also not shied away from prosecuting individuals who may be well-connected or, indeed, hold high positions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim has, in her speech, said that a Prosecutor must have no hesitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some examples of more recent and those further back prosecutions include actions against a Minister of State; against sitting and former Members of Parliament; against at that time, the Singapore Civil Defence Force Commissioner; the then-National Kidney Foundation Chief Executive Officer and also the then-Deputy Chief Executive of the Public Utilities Board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The public trust the Attorney-General and the broader legal system because we appoint individuals of the highest calibre and integrity and they exercise their discretions independently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The high levels of public trust in our legal system and the Attorney-General's Chambers speak for themselves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And he actually suggested also that the separation be introduced into the system as a matter of design, not because currently there are major issues now, but to pre-empt future problems, citing that, in other countries, pressure on prosecutors, perhaps by an unscrupulous Executive, is not unknown.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, from a systems design perspective, it is something that is good to consider.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The third point is that he mentioned that it is quite difficult to remove the Attorney-General and cited the Constitutional provisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: At the same time, the former Attorney-General who wrote the article highlighted a frequent change of Attorney-General does affect the morale of the Deputy Public Prosecutors (DPPs).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like the Senior Minister of State's comment on that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will address all three questions at the same time because I think they fundamentally centre on the question of trust in the independence of the Attorney-General and, of course, the functions of that office.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What other jurisdictions do, they do it for the reasons best known to themselves, or perhaps a design that is in response to the system that they themselves have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I highlighted the differences that I think Ms Sylvia Lim is very familiar with in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of the Attorneys-General hold political office, others have affiliations, and yet others, as Ms Sylvia Lim will be aware from my speech, also do not have security of tenure and go by a fixed term.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is different processes for different systems, and each country, each jurisdiction, must decide what works best.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In our context, we look at it from the perspective of what the broad institutional protections are in terms of the appointment, in terms of the removal, in terms of the fact that the Attorney-General has no political affiliation and holds no political office.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that I think is manifestly clear from the surveys that have been done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, yes, we constantly review this system that we have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand that other countries look at the separation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look at our system and we constantly evaluate it and we will make adjustments as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the end of the day, what drives the decisions that we make ultimately has to be the output, the performance and the way in which the public retains and reposes confidence in the functions of the Attorney-General.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Chairman, I do believe that this matter is worthy of further consideration, but at this juncture, in the interest of time, I would like to thank the Attorney-General's Chambers for its work and I beg leave to withdraw the amendment.
